t: The Act entitled “An Act in relation to contracts with the District of Columbia”, approved June 28, 1906 (34 Stat. 546), as amended by the Act approved June 26, 1912 (37 Stat. 168; D.C. Code, secs. 1–805 and 1–806) is amended by striking “$1,000” therefrom, and inserting in lieu thereof “$2,000”.

fable.w: This section only raises a dollar threshold in an existing statute on contracts with the District of Columbia, from $1,000 to $2,000. The tempting reading is that "contracts with the District of Columbia" implies coordination with outside parties, but the phrase is just the title of the amended Act, and contracting is not participation in a federal decision. The section creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, rulemaking or right to sue.
fable.s: is amended by striking “$1,000” therefrom, and inserting in lieu thereof “$2,000”

qwen_block.w: This section is a technical amendment to a statute regarding contract limits. It does not establish any process for consultation, public comment, advisory boards, or coordination with outside parties. It simply changes a monetary figure in existing law.
qwen_block.s: The Act entitled “An Act in relation to contracts with the District of Columbia”, approved June 28, 1906 (34 Stat. 546), as amended by the Act approved June 26, 1912 (37 Stat. 168; D.C. Code, secs. 1–805 and 1–806) is amended by striking “$1,000” therefrom, and inserting in lieu thereof “$2,000”.

opus.w: This section only raises a dollar threshold in the 1906 law on District of Columbia contracts, from $1,000 to $2,000. It creates no hearing, comment period, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to sue. Mentioning contracts doesn't count as participation, because contract awards are excluded and no outside party has a role in any federal decision here.
opus.s: is amended by striking “$1,000” therefrom, and inserting in lieu thereof “$2,000”.
opus.b: 1. **Thinking it through.** The words "contracts with the District of Columbia" might look like they involve outside parties. That reading doesn't hold up. The section only swaps one dollar amount for another in an existing law. It sets up no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation or right to sue. Contracting with outside parties is like an application or contract award, which the definition excludes.

qwen_chat.w: This section simply amends a monetary limit for contracts with the District of Columbia. It does not require or recommend any consultation, coordination, or participation by outside parties in the decision-making process. The District of Columbia is not involved in the decision to change the statutory cap; the change is made by Congress directly.
qwen_chat.s: The Act entitled “An Act in relation to contracts with the District of Columbia”, approved June 28, 1906 (34 Stat. 546), as amended by the Act approved June 26, 1912 (37 Stat. 168; D.C. Code, secs. 1–805 and 1–806) is amended by striking “$1,000” therefrom, and inserting in lieu thereof “$2,000”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing a dollar limit for contracts with the District of Columbia involves the District (an outside entity) in some way. However, the text merely amends a statutory cap on contract values; it does not establish a process for the District of Columbia or any other outside party to consult with, advise, or participate in federal decision-making. It is a simple appropriation/limitation amendment.
